title: The imam's role
hook: the imam leads prayer and teaches, with no priesthood between a person and Allah

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mosque community: a basement school, a committee, a sweeper missed by name. Your line was the mosque is people. Whom did you thank? Today, the one person who stands at the front. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-nine.

Three people are on a road trip and stop at a rest area when the time for prayer comes in. No mosque. No imam. One of them lays a jacket down on the grass to mark the direction. Then a small, friendly argument: you lead. No, you lead, you know more Qur'an. Finally one of them steps a pace forward, the other two line up behind, and the prayer begins. For those few minutes, that person is the imam. Then the prayer ends, and he's just the guy who's driving the next leg. Today, what an imam is, and what an imam isn't.
screen: `A REST AREA, A JACKET ON THE GRASS.` → `YOU LEAD. NO, YOU LEAD.` → `FOR A FEW MINUTES, THE IMAM.`

segments.voice: First, the job in its simplest form. In Sahih Muslim, Abu Mas'ud reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying, in paraphrase: the one who leads the people should be the one who best recites the Book of Allah, and if they're equal in that, the one who knows the Sunnah best. That's the qualification. Not a family line, not an ordination. Recitation and knowledge. So at a rest area, on a road trip, any qualified Muslim can lead. Second, the full-time imam. At a mosque, the imam usually leads the daily prayers, often gives the Friday sermon, teaches classes, marries couples, sits with grieving families and answers questions. A teacher and a pastor of sorts, in the everyday sense. Third, what the imam doesn't do. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh. I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me." The verse has Allah answering the one who calls, directly. The imam stands in front so the rows can pray together. He doesn't carry their prayers for them, and no one needs him present to pray. Another verse puts it closer still: "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." Fourth, a word with more than one size. The Qur'an uses it for Ibrahim: "Lo! I have appointed thee a leader for mankind." The Arabic there is imam. And Shia Muslims use Imam, with a capital I, for the Imams of the Prophet's family, a role far larger than leading a prayer. Same word, different weight, depending on who is speaking.
screen: `THE BEST RECITER LEADS.` · `TEACHER, PREACHER, NEIGHBOR.` · `I AM NIGH: NO ONE IN BETWEEN.` · `ONE WORD, DIFFERENT WEIGHTS.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray directly. Settle, and breathe. For these few minutes, set aside any waiting for the right person, the right building or the right words. Bring to mind one thing that's actually on your heart today. A worry, a thank-you, a question. If you pray, you can say it to Allah in your own words, silently, with no one in between, the way the verse describes: I am nigh. If you don't pray, simply put the thing into one plain sentence in your head and let it sit there, unhurried. The bell holds the time.
The imam's role. To lead the prayer, teach and serve, chosen for recitation and knowledge, standing in front of the rows, not between a person and Allah. Today's word.

Your line: no one in between. Today, whenever you wait for the right moment to say something that matters, to Allah or to a person, say it now instead. Tomorrow, the Deobandi and Barelvi traditions. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-nine.

original.note: Arabic: a leader; the one who leads the prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: the imam is a priest.
what it means: the one who stands in front to lead the prayer, and often teaches; chosen for recitation and knowledge, not standing between a person and Allah.
what a scholar hears: Abu Mas'ud's report in Muslim on who leads, al-Baqarah 2:186 on Allah being near, and imam used of Ibrahim in 2:124, with a larger meaning in Shia thought.

notes: This day needs a Shia reviewer as well: the script says Shia Muslims use 'Imam' for the Imams of the Prophet's family, 'a role far larger than leading a prayer', and frames 'no one in between' around the daily prayer. Shia teaching on the Imams' intercession and on religious authorities (marja') should be checked so the 'no one in between' line is fair to Shia Muslims.
Verify Pickthall's exact wording of 2:186, 50:16 and 2:124.
'A pastor of sorts, in the everyday sense' is meant descriptively; a Keeper may prefer different wording.
The duties of a full-time imam ('usually', 'often') are described without a cited source; confirm.
Editor: 'Muslims read this as' (a sweeping claim) changed to what the verse itself says; the practice no longer tells the listener what idea they hold.
